title: China Shipping: Typhoon Champi and US Port Pressure
metaDescription: Super Typhoon Champi threatens East China ports while US importers face stricter CBP rules and peak season price hikes on trans-Pacific lanes.
bottomLine: Super Typhoon Champi is the strongest storm of the year and threatens seven major Chinese airports and ports. US importers are simultaneously losing leverage with carriers as CBP tightens enforcement.

stories.headline: Super Typhoon Champi threatens East China gateways
stories.tldr: Super Typhoon Champi targets eastern China, risking disruptions at seven major airports including Shanghai Pudong and Ningbo Lishe.
stories.whatHappened:
Super Typhoon Champi is the strongest storm of the year worldwide. It is currently barreling towards Taiwan and mainland China, prompting authorities to plan evacuations and urge those in the storm's path to prepare for impact.

Aviation data platform VariFlight identifies seven airports at risk of disruption: Wenzhou Longwan, Fuzhou Changle, Ningbo Lishe, Hangzhou Xiaoshan, Shanghai Hongqiao, Shanghai Pudong, and Xiamen Gaoqi. Travellers and operators are bracing for potential closures across these major hubs.
stories.whyItMatters:
If you have stock sitting in warehouses in Ningbo or Shanghai, your window for getting it on a plane or ship is closing. Air freight is the first to go when these airports shut, and the backlog usually lasts a week after the storm passes. This creates a bottleneck that can stall your entire Q4 pipeline.

For those relying on just-in-time inventory for Q4, a three day shutdown at Pudong creates a ripple effect that hits your US or EU warehouse in mid-November. You will see a spike in spot rates as everyone tries to book the remaining capacity on alternative routes to avoid the storm zone.
stories.hotTake: Don't wait for the official airport closure notice. If your goods are ready, push them out of the storm zone now. I have seen 'potential disruptions' turn into total lockdowns in hours.
actions: Move urgent air shipments out of Shanghai and Ningbo before 24 October
Contact your forwarder to confirm the status of bookings for East China ports
Buffer your lead times by seven days for all East China departures this week

stories.headline: US importers lose leverage as CBP tightens rules
stories.tldr: US shippers face a combination of more stringent CBP regulations and rising peak season prices on eastbound trans-Pacific lanes.
stories.whatHappened:
Shippers report that US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is implementing more stringent rules for imports, increasing the pressure on those moving freight into the US. These regulatory moves are coinciding with the traditional peak season surge in demand.

At the same time, importers report dwindling leverage when negotiating with ocean carriers on the eastbound trans-Pacific route. Shippers describe a feeling of being under siege as they struggle to balance these tighter customs requirements with rising freight costs.
stories.whyItMatters:
You are being squeezed from both ends. Stricter CBP rules mean more detained shipments and higher chances of audits. If your paperwork is not perfect, your goods sit on the dock while you pay demurrage fees that eat your entire margin for that SKU.

Because carriers know you are desperate to hit Q4 sales, they are ignoring your volume discounts and historical relationships. You will pay the peak season premium whether you like it or not, and you have no one to turn to if your primary carrier drops your booking to make room for a higher payer.
stories.hotTake: The era of the 'preferred shipper' is over for mid-sized operators. Carriers only care about the big boxes now. You need to over-document every single shipment to avoid CBP delays.
actions: Audit your commercial invoices and packing lists for total accuracy to avoid CBP holds
Secure your November space now before carriers raise spot rates further
Diversify your carrier mix to avoid being held hostage by one line

stories.headline: Suez Canal returns for 63% of Far East-Europe capacity
stories.tldr: About 63% of ocean capacity between the Far East and Europe has returned to the Red Sea after three years of detours.
stories.whatHappened:
Alphaliner surveyed the 10 largest carrier networks over the past month to track capacity shifts. They found that vessels on 24 of 46 direct Far East-Europe services are now transiting the Red Sea, which accounts for 70% of the vessels on those specific services.

Overall, 63% of the total ocean capacity deployed on the lane has returned to the Suez route after three years of avoiding the area. Some operators are hedging against renewed disruption by maintaining several routes via the Cape of Good Hope.
stories.whyItMatters:
Transit times to Europe are dropping. You can stop padding your lead times by 14 days if your carrier is using the Suez route. This improves your cash flow by getting stock into your EU warehouses faster and reducing the time your capital is tied up in floating inventory.

However, the fact that some carriers are still hedging means you will see wildly different arrival dates for the same lane. You must check the specific vessel route, not the general lane average, or you will mismanage your warehouse labour and slot bookings in Europe.
stories.hotTake: The return to Suez is a gamble. Carriers are chasing efficiency, but one geopolitical spark puts you back on the long route. Keep a small percentage of your stock on the Cape route as insurance.
actions: Check your current vessel tracking to see if your cargo is routed via Suez or the Cape
Adjust your EU warehouse receiving schedules to account for shorter transit times
Compare transit times between your top three carriers for the China-Europe lane

stories.headline: China Merchants Port exits $392m Sri Lanka hub
stories.tldr: China Merchants Port Holdings has withdrawn from a $392 million joint venture to develop a logistics hub at Colombo Port.
stories.whatHappened:
The Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) announced that China Merchants Port Holdings decided not to proceed with a collaboration announced in 2023. The project was to develop a 150,000-square-metre logistics hub at Colombo Port.

China Merchants was to hold 70% of the joint venture, with the SLPA and a private construction company holding 15% each. The SLPA is now seeking a new investor. China Merchants already operates a $500m deep-water container terminal at the same port and manages the Hambantota port complex.
stories.whyItMatters:
While this is a corporate exit, it signals a shift in how Chinese state firms are assessing risk in South Asian infrastructure. If you route goods through Colombo as a transshipment point, be aware that the planned capacity expansion is now stalled.

This withdrawal follows a period of economic collapse in Sri Lanka. It suggests that even the largest Chinese players are prioritising 'commercial considerations' over strategic expansion. You should monitor whether this leads to further delays in regional hub efficiency or a shift in carrier routing patterns around the Indian Ocean.
stories.hotTake: Beijing is cleaning house. They are moving away from 'white elephant' projects and focusing on assets that actually return cash. If you were betting on Colombo becoming a massive new regional pivot, rethink your strategy.
actions: Review your transshipment hubs in South Asia for potential bottlenecks
Assess if your forwarder is relying on Colombo for regional distribution
Monitor for new investors in the Colombo logistics hub to gauge future capacity

faq.question: Which Chinese airports are affected by Typhoon Champi?
faq.answer: VariFlight identifies Wenzhou Longwan, Fuzhou Changle, Ningbo Lishe, Hangzhou Xiaoshan, Shanghai Hongqiao, Shanghai Pudong, and Xiamen Gaoqi as airports at risk.

faq.question: Are ships returning to the Suez Canal from China to Europe?
faq.answer: Yes. About 63% of ocean capacity on the Far East-Europe route has returned to the Red Sea and Suez Canal.

faq.question: Why are US importers struggling with trans-Pacific shipping right now?
faq.answer: Importers face stricter CBP rules and diminished leverage with ocean carriers during peak season price hikes.
